data.title: The oldest recipe for mead (14th century)
data.excerpt: Mead is regarded as a typically Slavic drink, one our ancestors were already drinking in Great Moravian times. No recipe from the 9th century has survived, but what is probably the oldest one that has – from a German book of the mid-14th century – is given here in full, along with a modern version anyone can try.

children.text: Mead is regarded as a typically Slavic alcoholic drink, one that our ancestors were already drinking in Great Moravian times, or even earlier. But what did such mead taste like then? What recipe did they use to make it? No recipe from the 9th century has survived. We have, however, managed to track down what is probably the oldest surviving recipe for this divine drink. The recipe was published in a German book and dates from the middle of the 14th century. So here you are – anyone who wishes may try it.
Mead (Das Buch von Guter Spise), Germany, 1346

blocks.text: Whoever would make good mead, let him warm clean spring water so that he may just dip his hand into it. And let him take two measures (3 l) of water and one (1.5 l) of honey. Let him mix them with a rod and leave it to stand a while, and then strain it through a clean cloth or through a hair sieve into a clean vessel. And then let him boil it for as long as it would take to cross an acre and come back again, and skim the froth from the wort with a bowl full of holes. The froth stays in the bowl and not in the wort. Next let him pour the mead into a clean cask and cover it so that the vapours cannot escape, until he is able to dip his hand into it. Then let him take a half-measure pot and fill it half full of hops and a handful of sage and boil that with the wort for as long as it would take to walk a mile, and let him take half a nut of fresh yeast and put it in and stir it, so that it ferments. Then let him likewise cover it so that the vapours may escape, for a day and a night. Then let him strain the mead through a clean cloth or through a hair sieve and pour it into a clean cask and leave it to ferment for three days and three nights, topping it up every evening. There let him leave it to settle and see to the topping up of the yeast. And let him leave it to rest for eight days so that it clears, topping it up every evening. Let him leave it to settle in a resined cask and leave it to rest for a full eight days, and let him drink of it for the first time after six to eight weeks. That, after all, is when it is at its best.
blocks.source: Das Buch von Guter Spise, 1346 (after the Czech translation)

blocks.alt: The oldest recipe for mead (14th century)

children.text: 1.5 l of honey, 3 l of water, about 0.4 l of hops, a handful of sage, yeast. Stir 1.5 litres of pure honey into 3 litres of warm water. Boil for 5 minutes and skim off the froth with a sieve. Take it off the heat and cover it with a lid. Into another pot put the hops and the sage, pour the still-warm honey decoction over them, stir well and boil for something like 1.5 hours, stirring all the while. Take it off the heat, stir in a teaspoon of yeast, put the lid on and leave it to ferment for 24 hours. Then strain it into a clean pot, add another teaspoon of yeast and set it aside for a further 24 hours. Do the same twice more. From the fifth to the twelfth day just crumble in yeast. On the thirteenth day strain it and leave it to rest for another 4–6 weeks. For the fermenting and the settling I recommend using stoneware or wooden vessels, for the sake of the taste.

blocks.text: Der guten mete machen wil, der werme reinen brunnen, daz er die hant dor inne liden künne. und neme zwei maz wazzers und eine honiges. daz rüere man mit eime stecken, und laz ez ein wile hangen. und sihe ez denne durch ein rein tuch oder durch ein harsip in ein rein vaz. und siede denne die selben wirtz gein eime acker lane hin und wider und schume die wirtz mit einer vensterehten schüzzeln. da der schume inne blibe und niht die wirtz. dor noch giuz den mete in ein rein vaz und bedecke in, daz der bradem niht uz müge, als lange daz man die hant dor inne geliden müge. So nim denne ein halp mezzigen hafen und tu in halp vol hopphen und ein hant vol salbey und siede daz mit der wirtz gein einer halben mile. und giuz ez denne in die wirtz, und nim frischer hoven ein halp nözzeln und giuz ez dor in. und giuz ez under ein ander daz ez geschende werde. so decke zu, daz der bradem iht uz müge einen tae und eine naht. So seige denne den mete durch ein reyn tuch oder durch ein harsip. und vazze in in ein reyn vaz und lazze in iern drie tac und drie naht und fülle in alle abende, dar nach lazze man in aber abe und hüete daz iht hefen dor in kumme und laz in aht tage ligen daz er valle. und fülle in alle abende. dar nach loz in abe in ein gehertztez vas und laz in ligen aht tage vol und trinke in denne erst sechs wucher oder ehte. so ist er allerbeste.
blocks.source: Das Buch von Guter Spise, 1346 (the original Middle High German text)

children.text: This cookery book was compiled some time between 1345 and 1354 by Michael de Leone, notary to the archbishop of Würzburg. In 1844 it was published in a Modern German translation. The book has two parts, the first containing 57 recipes and the second 44. It seems that these parts were joined together only subsequently. The first part in particular gives the impression of a self-contained text with a preface as well as a closing postscript. No further text follows this postscript; instead there is almost a third of a page of blank space. The next recipe then begins only on a new page. The dishes described were evidently not everyday fare, but rather festive ones. They often use more expensive ingredients, such as almonds, saffron, rice flour, white bread, large quantities of fat and the like. Most of them are pastries, puddings and desserts. The book was probably intended for a burgher readership.
The text is taken from a website on which all the other recipes from this remarkable book can also be found, so you can get cooking...
